title: Circuit hardness from inverse-polynomial-error BPP heuristics
formal: Does the uniform-distribution heuristic assumption \[\forall L\in\mathrm{BPP}\ \forall k\ge1\ \exists A_{L,k}\in\mathrm P\ \exists N_{L,k}\ \forall n\ge N_{L,k},\quad \Pr_{x\sim U_n}[A_{L,k}(x)\ne\mathbf1_L(x)]\le n^{-k}\] imply \[\mathrm{NEXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\quad\text{or}\quad\operatorname{Perm}\text{ has no polynomial-size arithmetic circuits over }\mathbb Z\] in the constant-free arithmetic-circuit model below?
why: Would clarify whether substantially weakening derandomization to allow a small set of bad inputs still forces nonuniform computational hardness. It probes the reach of the hardness-versus-randomness connection beyond exact or extremely low-error simulations.

sentences: The premise permits deterministic polynomial-time simulation of each BPP language with inverse-polynomial error under uniformly random inputs.
The guarantee holds at every sufficiently large length, with separate algorithms for different requested error powers.
The selected conclusion is a standard disjunction of Boolean circuit hardness for NEXP and arithmetic circuit hardness for the permanent.
An older theorem reaches this conclusion under much smaller exceptional sets.
The card makes the source’s broad converse direction precise through an explicitly authorized editorial specialization.

definitions: A language is a subset of \(\{0,1\}^*\); \(U_n\) is uniform on length-\(n\) binary strings. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized Turing machine in polynomial worst-case time on every random tape, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input and independent fair coins. Each \(A_{L,k}\) is one deterministic Turing machine with no advice and a worst-case polynomial time bound; its code, exponent and sufficiently-large-length threshold may depend on \(L,k\). No joint polynomial dependence on \(k\) is required. The displayed error is an input fraction at every sufficiently large length, not a probability over simulation coins. NEXP consists of languages recognized by nondeterministic Turing machines in time \(2^{n^a}\) for some fixed integer \(a\ge1\), allowing constant factors and finitely many small lengths. P/poly consists of languages whose length-\(n\) characteristic functions have polynomial-size Boolean circuits, with no uniformity between lengths. Boolean circuits are finite acyclic networks of fan-in-two AND and OR, unary NOT, input bits and constants, with one output. Circuit size is the length of an explicit binary gate-and-wire encoding. For \(m\ge1\), \(\operatorname{Perm}_m(X)=\sum_{\pi\in S_m}\prod_{i=1}^m X_{i,\pi(i)}\) is a formal polynomial in \(m^2\) indeterminates, where \(S_m\) is the set of permutations of \([m]\). Arithmetic circuits use fan-in-two addition, subtraction and multiplication, variable leaves and only the constants 0 and 1; there are no divisions or other field constants. They must compute the permanent as a formal polynomial over the integers, not merely on Boolean matrices. Polynomial size means one polynomial bound in \(m\) for all sufficiently large dimensions; the individual circuits need not be uniformly constructible. Thus a non-polynomial circuit conclusion excludes every fixed polynomial bound, rather than demanding an eventual exponential lower bound. The assertion is an ordinary logical implication, with no restriction to a black-box proof.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of this exact implication, or a Lean refutation establishing the heuristic premise together with polynomial-size circuits for every NEXP language and for the permanent in the stated arithmetic model. An unconditional proof of either circuit lower-bound conclusion suffices. A uniform time-class separation, a different simulation premise or an impossibility restricted to a chosen proof method does not settle the assertion.

context_blocks.text: The original paper asks broadly whether its inverse-polynomial-error heuristics force any nonuniform circuit lower bounds. It leaves the precise consequence unspecified.

With the user’s authorization, this card selects the standard Boolean-or-permanent circuit-hardness disjunction from the cited typically-correct derandomization theorem, and fixes the deterministic uniform-distribution premise. This is an editorial specialization of the broad converse question.

The older theorem obtains this disjunction with a much smaller exceptional set of encodings. An inverse-polynomial fraction permits many more exceptional inputs, so its hypothesis cannot simply be substituted here.
